title: Romans agree the just can have some certainty without special revelation; they differ on its kind
source_text: XIV. His ita expositis, inter omnes Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae convenit, eos qui vere fideles & justi sunt, posse de propria gratia aliquo modo certos esse, & ad aliquam veram & legitimam de remissione peccatorum suorum, & sua coram Deo justificatione, certitudinem pervenire, etiam citra ullam specialem revelationem. Sed quae & qualis sit illa certitudo, & ad quod genus pertineat, inter eos non constat, & quaedam est in eorum Scholis sententiarum hac de re diversitas. Ut videre est apud Bellarminum, lib. 3. de Justif. cap. 11. §. Tres enim; ubi dicit inter Catholicos tres numerari de hac quaestione sententias.
pass_a_gloss: These things thus set out, among all the doctors of the Roman Church it is agreed that those who are truly faithful and just can in some way be certain of their own grace, and can arrive at some true and legitimate certainty concerning the remission of their sins and their justification before God, even apart from any special revelation. But what and of what sort that certainty is, and to what kind it belongs, is not settled among them, and there is a certain diversity of opinions on this matter in their Schools. As may be seen in Bellarmine, On Justification, book 3, chapter 11, section ‘For three’; where he says that among Catholics three opinions on this question are numbered.
pass_b_english: All Roman doctors grant the truly just some real certainty of grace without special revelation.
They disagree on its grade; Bellarmine counts three Catholic opinions.
